title: Before New York Mandates Evidence-Based Math
author: Lippert, Samantha
summary: Yesterday was my last day in the classroom before summer, and while I was packing up my things, I did something I should have done a long time ago. I took Jo Boaler's Mindset Mathematics curriculum guide off my bookshelf, walked out into the hallway, and tossed it right onto the trash pile. For years, that book sat on my shelf like a security blanket. I wanted my kids to love math, to be confident, and I bought into the idea that "productive struggle" was the magic key. But this past year, I completely flipped my classroom. I threw out the trendy frameworks, looked at actual cognitive science, and changed everything about how I teach. I'm never going back to what she pushed--or to what the New York State Education Department (NYSED) is pushing now under the guise of their new "Back to Basics in Math" initiative. It reflects many of the same underlying assumptions, just now carrying the authority of a state agency. On paper, New York's new law looks like a win. After years of watching student math scores tank, the state is finally admitting that instruction matters. But if you look closely at what NYSED is actually rolling out--and at New York Focus's recent reporting on the rollout--we are about to make the exact same disastrous mistakes we just spent years trying to fix in reading reform. I'm not writing this because one 18-student classroom can settle a massive research debate. It can't. I'm writing because my classroom became a small test case for two competing instructional philosophies. The results don't just raise important questions about the assumptions shaping New York's definition of "evidence-based" instruction; they show exactly what the alternative looks like when put into practice. Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. What "Productive Struggle" Looks Like From the Front of the Room I have taught Ready Classroom Mathematics for years largely as written. Most lessons opened the exact same way most inquiry-aligned curricula do: students received a complex problem before anyone had demonstrated how to solve it. The intended purpose was to let them grapple. The daily reality looked entirely different. Instead of an inspired mathematical workshop, I watched a room split in two. A few students who already possessed enough background knowledge to begin reasoning engaged with the problem. The rest froze. They guessed. They stared at the paper. They looked around the room hoping someone else knew what to do, waiting for me to arrive. By the time I reached them, the instructional sequence had already broken down. The issue wasn't that the math was too hard. The issue was that we were asking kids to be flexible with knowledge they hadn't even learned yet. Confusion is not the same thing as productive struggle. You can't tell the difference between the two from a state policy brief, but you sure can tell when you're watching 18 kids fail to even write down a single number. From the perspective of cognitive science, this mismatch becomes blindingly obvious. Learning typically progresses through four predictable stages: Acquisition: Where a skill is first learned. Fluency: Where it becomes automatic. Generalization: Where it transfers to new contexts. Adaptation: Where it can be flexibly applied to solve novel problems. Yet inquiry-first lessons routinely ask students to operate at the adaptation stage before they have completed basic acquisition. For my students with Individualized Education Programs (IEPs), and for plenty of general education students as well, that isn't a productive struggle. It is working memory getting entirely overloaded and burned on uncertainty instead of actual learning. What We Changed My co-teacher and I made one decisive choice early this school year: keep the Ready Math content, but completely throw out the instructional sequence. Explicit First: We taught the concept explicitly before students were ever asked to apply or manipulate it. Continuous Checks: We checked for understanding continuously--using dry-erase whiteboards, choral response, and targeted turn-and-talks--instead of releasing students to independent work just because a lesson plan script said it was time. Daily Fluency: Outside of the core math block, we added four minutes a day of explicit, mastery-based math fact practice for every student, at every level, moving up the same systematic skill ladder. That last piece matters specifically because it is the exact practice NYSED's current guidance is most skeptical of. Automaticity with math facts is treated, in the inquiry-aligned framing, as secondary to conceptual understanding--something that supposedly follows naturally if you just teach for meaning. Our experience proved the exact opposite. When a student doesn't have to pause, count on their fingers, or burn mental energy trying to calculate a basic fact like 7x8, that cognitive space goes somewhere invaluable. It goes toward understanding what a number line represents, or holding a two-step word problem in working memory long enough to map out a solution. I watched a student pause mid-problem this past spring and tell me, completely unprompted: "I just realized I have to use all my math facts together to solve this. I couldn't even see what the problem was asking without them." We didn't abandon conceptual math. We built a foundation so kids actually had the cognitive space to do it. Students first acquired a procedure through explicit instruction, practiced until it was reasonably fluent, and only then were asked to explain their reasoning, compare strategies, and apply what they knew to unfamiliar problems. Conceptual understanding wasn't replaced--it was built on a foundation that freed up the mental energy kids needed to actually reason. What the Numbers Actually Show To evaluate if our changes were working, we tracked two separate measures: i-Ready, the district-required digital diagnostic, and Acadience Math, a pencil-and-paper benchmark we added ourselves. We needed Acadience because digital diagnostics provide a broad, abstract scale score, but offer zero visibility into a student's literal, raw scratchwork. From fall to winter, every single student present for both Acadience benchmarks improved--several of them dramatically. One student's composite score leaped from 22 to 125; several others nearly tripled their scores. When looking at the share of students scoring at or above grade-level expectations, the steady upward climb was undeniable: Computation Strand: Climbed from 56% of students at Benchmark 1, to 78% at Benchmark 2, and settled at 72% by Benchmark 3. Concepts & Applications Strand: Rose steadily from 56% to 67% across the same window. i-Ready's scale scores told a similar story once we looked at student distributions rather than hiding behind a flat classroom average: Overall Proficiency: In the fall, only 3 of 17 students (18%) scored in the on-track "green" range. By spring, 12 of 18 students (66%) did. Numbers and Operations Strand: Growth here was even sharper, jumping from 4 of 17 students (24%) on track in the fall to 14 of 18 students (78%) by spring. The Danger of a Single Metric The data also revealed a crucial nuance at the individual level, proving exactly why relying on a single data measure is dangerous. One of our hardest-working students completely mastered her foundational math facts--her Acadience fluency composite nearly tripled--yet her district-mandated adaptive test score didn't budge. Why? Because learning isn't a linear conveyor belt. She is in a fragile, transitional phase where her newly acquired fluency hasn't yet translated into complex, multi-step problem-solving. Had we relied solely on the state-approved adaptive software, we might have concluded our instruction had failed her. If my district forces me to pace my class strictly by state-certified guidelines, I am forced to choose between supporting her current, messy developmental reality and teaching to the test's timeline. True evidence-based analysis requires the humility to look at discrepancies like this one rather than flattening them into a clean policy win. My classroom doesn't prove that every inquiry-first approach fails everywhere, or that explicit instruction is a magic bullet. But it does demonstrate that explicit teaching combined with systematic fluency practice can produce massive, rapid growth in the exact kind of classroom often assumed to benefit most from inquiry-based methods. What NYSED Is Actually Telling Teachers The new law mandates that the State Education Department define "evidence-based" practices by January, with full district alignment required by 2027. So far, the clearest look at what NYSED considers "evidence-based" comes from eight instructional briefs written by Deborah Loewenberg Ball and her TeachingWorks team at the University of Michigan. The briefs are deeply ideological. They push heavily for mathematical discussion and inquiry while explicitly warning teachers against timed fact drills or grading for speed, claiming they cause math anxiety. Those recommendations have not gone unchallenged. More than 200 mathematics researchers, educators, and parents signed a petition asking NYSED to withdraw the briefs, arguing that they misrepresent the research on fluency, explicit instruction, and mathematical learning. When Ball published her defense, she essentially dodged the core critique. Instead of addressing the actual issue--sequencing--she reframed the argument, acting as if her critics were entirely against kids understanding concepts. Nobody is saying conceptual understanding doesn't matter. We are saying that kids need explicit instruction and foundational fluency before they can execute high-level mathematical reasoning. The petition's specific charge was that the briefs minimize explicit instruction and automaticity. Ball's defense was that the briefs never claimed timed tests were the only cause of anxiety, or that drills were the only way to build fluency--claims nobody actually made. This remains a highly contested position to codify into law, especially for a state that currently ranks 38th in the nation for 4th-grade math. As a classroom teacher, I can tell you that this inquiry-first philosophy simply does not survive contact with a room full of real children. The 200+ signatories of that petition aren't cartoon villains trying to turn kids into rote calculators. They are pointing out that cognitive science and math education research are in the middle of a massive, unresolved debate about sequencing. By turning one specific, highly contested academic camp into state law, NYSED is treating a philosophical preference as settled scientific consensus. Meanwhile, landmark, peer-reviewed work like Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark's 2006 paper "Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work," along with the Institute of Education Sciences' (IES) own Practice Guides, points the other way. Both emphasize systematic error correction and timed, low-stakes retrieval practice alongside conceptual visuals--the exact combination NYSED's briefs treat with deep suspicion. I Already Watched This Philosophy Fail Once None of these ideas were unfamiliar to me. The Mindset Mathematics series I just threw away built its reputation on the exact same instincts now appearing in NYSED's guidance: de-emphasize speed and procedure, minimize ability grouping, delay explicit teaching, and trust that conceptual understanding will naturally emerge if students are given the right kind of struggle. For years, I found those ideas deeply compelling because it's an appealing story to tell. Then I started looking more closely at the evidence--not just the conclusions researchers reported, but the data used to justify the very curriculum products sold to districts. Researcher Rahim Nathwani documented significant concerns with a widely cited YouCubed case study - the same organization behind the Mindset Mathematics books - that claimed dramatic district-wide gains in California. The published claims did not align with publicly available state achievement data, and later revisions substituted a single school's data for district-wide results without clearly disclosing the change. Years earlier, Stanford mathematicians had raised similar methodological concerns about Boaler's highly influential 2008 Railside study, pointing out critical issues regarding its transparency and peer verification. I don't bring those examples up to relitigate Jo Boaler's career. I bring them up because they illustrate a larger principle: educational philosophies deserve the same level of scientific scrutiny we expect from any other empirical claim, especially when they begin shaping statewide policy. The same healthy skepticism appears in Holly Korbey's reporting on the growing number of schools and districts reconsidering productive struggle as a daily instructional default. Daniel OK-Carr reaches similar conclusions in his analysis of i-Ready Classroom Mathematics, tracing the research often cited to justify daily productive struggle and demonstrating that much of it simply does not support routine, unguided problem-solving for novice elementary learners. Different authors, different evidence, but the same underlying question: Have we become far more confident about productive struggle than the actual research warrants? Why This Should Worry Anyone Watching the Rollout The New York Focus reporting makes it clear that NYSED's guidance is not a neutral synthesis of settled, consensus science. It represents one highly specific side of an intense, active debate. The reading reform initiative this math law is modeled after already showed us what happens when state guidance is overly broad and compliance relies on districts self-certifying. Many districts reported using curricula that cognitive scientists argued were entirely inconsistent with the science of reading, while still claiming full compliance on paper. Math reform risks repeating this exact loop if the state's foundational guidance remains highly contested and independent verification remains practically non-existent. There's a more specific parallel worth naming, too. The "Back to Basics in Math" budget sets aside $2 million for the state teachers' union to run a training course on these new standards. New York already ran this exact playbook with reading: the 2024 law set aside $10 million to retrain 20,000 teachers, and handed that money to New York State United Teachers to develop the course. The union launched it last September. But according to the Times Union, literacy experts who reviewed the course found it leaned heavily on the outdated "balanced literacy" approach Hochul's own reform was supposed to retire. An NYU professor reviewed a sample of the slides and didn't hold back: "There are just lots of inaccuracies and very old citations. We've spent $10 million on this? Can I get a refund?" Handing curriculum training right back to the same institutional infrastructure that helped create the bad habits in the first place isn't a minor implementation detail. It's a structural reason to doubt that "evidence-based" training will look any different on the ground than what's already failing students. The Staffing Spotlights an Equity Blind Spot Heading into the NY state testing this school year, my general education students were projected at 83% to 92% proficiency--well above New York's current statewide average. After seeing how they actually performed on the actual test, I think that projection will hold true. I even think one of my students got every single question correct on the test. I know this is just one 18-student classroom, but it is the largest in our building--in a district where 85% of students qualify as economically disadvantaged and one-third of my classroom's students receive special education services. It is easy to look at our results and say "explicit instruction works." But my classroom had a luxury most in New York do not: 18 students and two co-teachers. With a roughly 9:1 ratio, we could run continuous whiteboard checks and catch misconceptions instantly. If an inquiry-first curriculum requires this level of intensive staffing to keep struggling students from drowning in "productive struggle," that is an equity failure. If an explicit sequence relies on it to ensure students aren't just passively copying steps, we need to know that too. NYSED's briefs say almost nothing about how physical classroom conditions--staffing ratios, co-teaching, class size--dictate whether a given sequence can even be implemented as designed. No single classroom can eliminate every environmental variable. But the most significant, intentional instructional change we made this year was replacing an inquiry-first sequence with explicit teaching, continuous checks for understanding, and systematic fluency practice. Those choices directly coincided with the strongest mathematics outcomes I have ever seen in my 18 years of teaching. To be clear, I don't think conceptual understanding and procedural fluency are competing goals. Students absolutely should explain their thinking, reason mathematically, make connections, and solve unfamiliar problems. The question isn't whether those things matter. The question is when students are developmentally ready to do them independently. Sequencing matters. The cognitive science literature suggests that flexible reasoning is built on a foundation of knowledge and automaticity, not as a substitute for them. My classroom cannot establish causation, and it certainly doesn't settle a statewide debate. But it does provide something policy discussions often lack: a detailed example of what happened when one classroom deliberately reversed the instructional sequence promoted by many inquiry-oriented programs. The results don't tell us what every classroom should do. They do suggest that explicit instruction and systematic fluency practice deserve a far more prominent place in New York's definition of evidence-based mathematics instruction than the current guidance appears willing to give them. Students who arrive at school with strong background knowledge often succeed despite imperfect instruction.
